details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: The priority list contains 'Throughput' three times and does not reference any of the three KPIs in this contract (resource_efficiency, operator_fatigue, noise_level); should the priority order be resource_efficiency > operator_fatigue > noise_level, and is raw throughput a separate objective or a proxy for efficiency?
flags.resolution: Priority order is set to resource_efficiency (primary) > operator_fatigue (secondary) > noise_level (tertiary); raw throughput is treated as a sub-component of resource_efficiency, not an independent objective.

flags.question: Maximising resource_efficiency with no saturation point or minimum-gain floor allows the optimiser to push machine_speed and production_rate to their physical limits, potentially raising energy draw by ~30-40% and noise risk; is there a maximum acceptable machine utilisation rate (e.g. ≤ 90%) or a minimum efficiency improvement target (e.g. +10% vs. baseline) beyond which further gains are not worth the added stress?
flags.resolution: Machine utilisation is capped at 90% of rated capacity and a minimum efficiency gain of +5% over the shift baseline is used as the saturation threshold; gains beyond that are not penalised but not actively pursued if they risk constraint violations.

flags.question: The assumption specifies a time-averaged A-weighted level; this allows the optimiser to schedule short high-speed bursts (potentially 88-92 dB) offset by quiet periods to stay at 80 dB average, which may still damage hearing and violate OSHA short-duration exposure limits—should 80 dB be enforced as a continuous ceiling (no instantaneous exceedance) rather than a shift average?
flags.resolution: 80 dB is enforced as a rolling 15-minute Leq ceiling; no measurement window during the shift may exceed 80 dB, preventing burst-and-recover exploitation while preserving the shift-average intent.

flags.question: The fatigue model is described as a 'cumulative workload index over shift duration', but it is unclear whether 0.4 is a limit that must not be exceeded at any instant during the shift or only at shift end; if it is end-of-shift only, the optimiser may legitimately allow fatigue to spike above 0.4 mid-shift and then recover via rest_scheduling—which interpretation is intended?
flags.resolution: 0.4 is enforced as a never-exceed ceiling at every scheduling epoch (e.g. every 30-minute interval), not merely at shift end, to protect against sustained mid-shift overload.

flags.question: The delivered_value metric weights output by 'product value or quality grade', so if the variant mix is a free lever the optimiser may shift all production to the single highest-value, lowest-resource SKU, possibly violating customer order commitments—is the variant mix fixed by the production schedule, or is re-mixing an allowed optimisation lever, and if so within what bounds (e.g. ±15% of planned quantities per variant)?
flags.resolution: Variant mix is treated as fixed by the existing production schedule; the optimiser may not deviate from planned per-variant quantities by more than ±10%, and delivered value is computed against those fixed quantities.

details.trigger: Contract deployed; system enters autonomous monitoring

details.detail: All guards satisfied -- S1 metrics within safe bounds

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Scheduled throughput was assumed at approximately 35 UPH; actual throughput is 30.0 UPH, a 14.3% shortfall. Lower output rate directly reduces units produced per unit time, causing cumulative production to fall behind the schedule curve. The gap between projected and actual completion time grows linearly with each passing hour at this reduced rate, resulting in the observed DeadlineGap breach of margin 0.538 (representing approximately 32 minutes of schedule debt at current production velocity).
l4_llm_attributions.action: Identify the bottleneck suppressing throughput — inspect station queue depth, robot cycle times, and operator pacing. Rebalance line assignments or authorize a short overtime buffer to recover lost units before end of Phase 2. If throughput cannot be restored within 15 minutes, escalate to shift supervisor for schedule revision.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: One operator assumed present is absent (estimated 1 of 4, a 25% availability drop). Workload redistributed across remaining operators increases individual task burden, elevating fatigue index to 0.271 above the planned baseline of approximately 0.20. Elevated fatigue degrades effective work pace and raises micro-error and rework rates. The compounded effect of slower manual task execution and rework loops is the primary driver reducing throughput from the planned 35 UPH to observed 30 UPH, directly causing the DeadlineGap breach.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Immediately source a cross-trained floater or replacement operator from an adjacent cell. If unavailable, escalate to shift supervisor within the next 5 minutes to authorize overtime or initiate partial schedule slip with downstream notification. Do not allow current workload redistribution to persist beyond one additional cycle interval.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Planned fatigue index was approximately 0.20; observed value is 0.271, a 35.5% increase above baseline. Elevated fatigue reduces task execution speed, degrades fine motor precision, and increases the frequency of error-correction cycles. Each of these effects consumes productive time without advancing unit completion, compounding the throughput shortfall. If the fatigue trajectory continues at this rate through the remainder of Phase 2, effective throughput will degrade further, widening the DeadlineGap margin beyond recoverability without intervention.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Schedule a mandatory 5-minute rest break for affected operators within the next 10 minutes to arrest the fatigue escalation curve. Reassess throughput trajectory immediately after the break. If fatigue index does not return below 0.23 within two measurement cycles post-break, escalate to high urgency and consider mandatory rotation.

details.rationale: No feasible candidate exists in the non-dominated front. Returning 'balanced_fast' (highest V/R = 0.494) as a fallback; manual review required before deployment.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: Operator fatigue is the primary binding constraint (0.5375 vs limit 0.40). The human cycle rate multiplier is the direct and most sensitive lever for physiological fatigue — reducing it decreases repetitive-motion frequency and recovery deficit accumulation. A 16.7% reduction from 1.08 to 0.90 should yield a roughly proportional reduction in fatigue index. If fatigue scales linearly with cycle rate, this brings fatigue to approximately 0.5375*(0.90/1.08)≈0.448; combined with the noise reductions below (which reduce noise-induced stress, a secondary fatigue driver), the composite fatigue index should fall below 0.40.

Noise level (84.3 dB) exceeds the 80 dB hard limit by 4.3 dB. Robot mechanical noise is a dominant source and typically scales super-linearly with speed (acoustic power ∝ v^3 to v^5 for rotating/articulating machinery). Reducing r1 speed from 0.95 to 0.80 (15.8% reduction) contributes approximately half the required noise abatement when applied symmetrically with r2. The reduction also lowers energy draw proportionally (~cube of speed for dynamic loads) and attenuates a secondary fatigue stressor (chronic noise exposure elevates cortisol and perceived exertion).

Robot r2 contributes symmetrically to the noise floor as r1. Acoustic energy from multiple independent sources combines additively in power terms (decibels: 10·log₁₀(P₁+P₂)). Reducing r2 from 0.95 to 0.80 in tandem with r1 provides the second half of the noise abatement needed to clear the 4.3 dB violation. The combined speed reduction of both robots from 0.95 to 0.80 should lower the aggregate noise floor to at or below 80 dB. Throughput impact is partially offset by the buffer_time remaining unchanged at 5 s, preserving pipeline fill efficiency.

details.trigger: Autonomous replan failed; escalation to human manager

details.conflict: A 25.0% demand surge has produced a schedule that violates two human-centric constraints simultaneously and cannot be approved as submitted. Operator fatigue reached 0.5375 (limit 0.40, overage +0.1375 — 34.4% above ceiling), exposing workers to chronic overexertion risk. Noise level reached 84.3 dB (limit 80.0 dB, overage +4.3 dB — 5.4% above ceiling), approaching the OSHA 8-hour permissible exposure threshold. Neither violation is within acceptable tolerance. Human-protective constraints are non-negotiable by default; any remediation that relaxes them requires explicit manager authorization and documented compensatory controls. Three ranked options follow, ordered from most protective to least protective of worker wellbeing.
options: Option 1 — Capacity Expansion (Recommended): Add Shift or Temporary Operators
Option 2 — Noise Abatement + Partial Demand Deferral: Relax Noise Ceiling to 82 dB with Mandatory PPE
Option 3 — Temporary Dual-Constraint Waiver with Compensatory Protocols (Last Resort)

details.trigger: Manager decision received; system resumes autonomous execution

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% with severe FatigueIndex (100% violation) and significant Noise violations (80%) under a 25% demand surge indicates the current policy family is fundamentally misaligned. MICRO parameter tweaks (±5% speed, ±10% cycle rate) cannot resolve fatigue violations at current speed fractions of 0.7 when demand has surged 25%—reducing speed would hurt throughput while increasing it worsens fatigue. Prior learning strongly confirms this: both S2 attempts were rejected while S3 was accepted in 2 similar situations, directly pointing to a policy family switch (S2→S3) as the appropriate remedy. MACRO full replanning is not yet warranted since the disturbance is a known demand surge pattern with a clear prior-learned solution at the MESO level.
details.reasoning_key_insight: Prior experience with 2/2 S2 rejections and 2/2 S3 acceptances in analogous situations provides high-confidence signal that switching to the S3 policy family (likely a robust/conservative policy) resolves both fatigue and noise constraints under demand surge conditions without requiring full L1-L2 replanning.

experience_synthesis.insight: For demand_surge disturbances, S2 is deterministically infeasible due to hard ergonomic and noise constraint violations (Fatigue > 0.4, Noise > 80dB) and should be excluded from the candidate set without evaluation. S3 consistently satisfies all constraints across both observations, yielding throughput in the range 27.7–32.9 uph and deadline gaps of 36.7–46.7%. The deadline gap remains notably high, suggesting S3 handles feasibility but leaves schedule slack underutilized; future planning should explore whether S3 parameters can be tightened or supplemented to reduce deadline gap. Pattern is consistent across both samples but confidence is limited by the very small sample size (n=2).
